note: A dramatized adaptation for distinct character voices. Dialogue is newly rendered from the poem and this retelling; it is not a literal manuscript translation. The paired verse excerpts remain separately identified.

turns.text: Odin stood before the seeress, a woman whose memory reached beyond the beginnings of his rule. He had come seeking knowledge.
Tell me what you remember. Speak of the world's beginning, and what is yet to come.

Then listen, great and small, children of Heimdall. I remember a world older than your power, Odin. In my sight, what has happened and what must happen stand close together. You ask for knowledge. I will give it to you, but I promise no comfort.
I remember the giants who fostered me long ago, and nine worlds beneath the earth. In that first age there was no shore to stand on, no cool waves coming in, no heaven raised above a field of grass.

Then the sons of Borr lifted the land and shaped the human dwelling of Midgard. Sunlight reached the stones from the south, and green growth covered the ground. Sun, moon, and stars did not yet know their places. The gods sat in council and named the divisions of time: morning, evening, and the reckoning of years.

At Iðavöllr they built high sanctuaries and halls. They established forges, made tongs, and worked metal. In the grass they played with golden gaming pieces, possessing gold without anxiety about its lack. Then three powerful giant women arrived.

The first age does not last. The vision shifts, leaving some connections unexplained. Its hearers are expected to recognize fragments of a much larger store of stories. But the golden pieces lying in the grass will return to the seeress's vision before she is done.

Now come the dwarfs, named in a long roll call. Mótsognir and Durinn stand at its beginning; many others follow. Their names suggest directions, objects, powers, and qualities. The catalogue remembers the inhabitants of the world, not merely its rulers.

Then three gods found Ask and Embla on the land. They had no settled destiny, no breath or understanding of their own. You gave them breath, Odin. Hœnir gave understanding, and Lóðurr gave warmth and good colour.
Human life begins as a giving of powers. The precise force of some of those ancient words remains uncertain; the gifts themselves are unmistakable.

Above these beginnings stands the ash Yggdrasill, nourished by pale moisture, its dew falling into valleys. Beneath it are the women who determine lives. Urðr, Verðandi, and Skuld establish laws, choose lives, and set the fates of human beings.
Even when the world seems newly furnished, its inhabitants have limits. The gods can shape land and confer life. The poem does not say that they can simply order fate to disappear.

I remember the first war. Gullveig was pierced with spears and burned in the High One's hall: three times burned, three times born, still living. Heiðr practised powerful magic. The gods debated responsibility and compensation. You cast a spear into the host, Odin. The defences of the Æsir broke, and the Vanir trod the field.

The relation between Gullveig and Heiðr is suggested rather than explained. In another compressed scene the gods ask who has promised Freyja to the giants. Thor rises in anger, and solemn agreements are broken. Divine society has entered the world of violence and damaged oaths.
I know where you have hidden your eye, Odin, in Mímir's famous well. You came to me alone and offered rings and necklaces for knowledge. Would you know more?

She sees secrets as well as public disasters. Her recurring question presses him onward. The answer costs him nothing as simple as money. The knowledge he seeks includes his own destruction, and every new image brings that destruction nearer.

I see valkyries ready to ride. I see Baldr, your son, within the reach of death. A slender mistletoe shoot becomes the weapon Höðr will use. A brother born to avenge Baldr acts while scarcely a day old. He will not wash his hands or comb his hair before the killing is answered. Frigg weeps in Fensalir.
These incidents arrive in swift, hard flashes. The poem does not recount all the familiar details supplied elsewhere about the gods' games or the promises gathered from every living thing.

A bound figure resembling Loki lies with unhappy Sigyn beside him. Rivers run through poisoned valleys. Far from the sun stands a hall with doors facing north and walls woven with serpents. There I see oath-breakers and murderers enduring punishment. In Ironwood a giant woman breeds wolves. One of their kin will take the heavenly light.
Danger is gathering in the creatures, halls, and borders around the gods. It is no longer confined to quarrels inside their assembly.

A red cock crows among the giants. Gullinkambi wakes Odin's warriors, and another cock cries below the earth. Garmr howls before Gnipahellir. Bonds strain and break. Brothers kill brothers. Cousins destroy the obligations of kinship. Would you know more?

The warning travels through different realms. The approaching ruin is also a collapse of the relationships that made life within the world possible. The seeress names an age of axes and swords, of wind and wolves.

Heimdall raises the Gjallarhorn. You consult Mímir's head, Odin, while the old ash shakes and its branches tremble. Hrymr advances with his shield. The great serpent churns the sea. Naglfar is loose, and Loki comes with the force approaching over the water.
Surtr comes from the south carrying destructive fire, his sword shining like the sun. Rocks break, beings crowd the road to Hel, and the sky itself is torn apart.
The vision moves between armies and landscapes as though the entire world has become one battlefield.

You meet the wolf, Odin, and you fall. Víðarr comes to avenge his father, driving his sword into the monster's heart. Freyr, the slayer of Beli, confronts Surtr. Thor kills the world-serpent, but victory does not save him. He takes nine steps before sinking beneath its venom.

These are not defeats caused by a failure to fight bravely. The defenders do what their identities demand, and the world still ends. The sun blackens; the earth sinks into the sea; stars vanish and fire reaches heaven.

Yet I see the earth rise again, green from the water. Waterfalls run. An eagle flies above them and catches fish beneath the cliffs. At Iðavöllr the gods who remain speak of the great serpent and remember the old powers. They find the golden gaming pieces in the grass.

The quiet objects of the first age return after the noise of its destruction. Unsown fields bear crops. Baldr and Höðr are together again, no longer held apart by the killing that defined their former lives.
A hall roofed with gold stands brighter than the sun, offering dwelling and happiness. But there comes Níðhöggr, the dark dragon, flying with corpses upon his wings. Now I must sink.

She does not explain away this last image or turn her prophecy into an untroubled promise. Odin has heard the making of a world, the breaking of its bonds, and the possibility of another beginning. The voice that showed him all this withdraws, leaving him with knowledge rather than escape.
